name: Chapman's Blue
lede: Chapman's Blue is a muted, mid-toned blue from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary, named for a person whose identity Ridgway never records.

sections.title: A surname without a story
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 “Color Standards and Color Nomenclature” lists Chapman's Blue at hex #5C729E among the names he credits to a person, rather than a place, dye or pigment [1]. Chapman is a common English surname, and Ridgway gives no first name, trade or date for his, so which Chapman the color honors is undocumented in our sources [1]. The 1955 Inter-Society Color Council catalog repeats the name in the block it calls moderate blue [1].

Its nearest neighbor in our color graph is [[jay-blue|Jay Blue]], only 2.6 units away and almost the same [1]. [[stardew|Stardew]] sits almost as close, and [[azure-blue|Azure Blue]] is a near match as well [1]. Against the basic color words it reads closest to [[denim|Denim]], 8.1 units off, a cleaner, less grey blue than Chapman's own [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive matches this blue in 0.54% of 23,781 paintings, 128 of them, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 64 [2]. That makes it more common than 53% of the named colors in our set [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 0.5% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 1.4 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 58% of its 64 appearances, by lightness rank rather than by brand [2]. Titian is its most devoted painter here, holding it in 4 of 50 works, 6.2 times the baseline of the museums those paintings come from [2]. Our earliest match dates to 1426, by Fra Angelico, 486 years before Ridgway's 1912 book recorded the name, a floor rather than a first, since a color match in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment [2].
